learning_objective: 🎯 Master Python's most powerful built-in data structures to store, manipulate, and retrieve collections of data dynamically.

key_vocabulary.definition: An ordered, mutable sequence of elements enclosed in square brackets [ ].
An unordered, mutable collection of key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces { }.
An object whose state or contents can be changed after it is created.
The numerical position of an element in a sequence, starting from 0.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Lists hold multiple items in a specific order: `marks = [85, 90, 78]`. You can access items by index (`marks[0]` is 85). Lists are mutable, meaning you can change elements (`marks[0] = 88`) without creating a new list.

Lists have powerful methods: `.append(x)` adds to the end, `.insert(index, x)` adds at a specific spot, `.pop()` removes the last item, and `.remove(x)` deletes a specific value. You can also 'slice' lists to get sub-parts: `marks[1:3]`.

Dictionaries don't use numerical indexes; they use 'Keys'. Think of a real dictionary where the word is the Key and the definition is the Value. `student = {'name': 'Rahul', 'age': 17}`. You access values using their keys: `student['name']` gives 'Rahul'.

Keys must be unique and immutable (like strings or numbers). Values can be anything (even lists!). Add new pairs easily: `student['grade'] = 'A'`. Useful methods include `.keys()`, `.values()`, and `.items()`.

fun_activity.title: ✂️ The Slicing Ninja
fun_activity.instructions: Let `colors = ['Red', 'Green', 'Blue', 'Yellow', 'Pink']`. What does `colors[1:4]` output? It starts at index 1 ('Green') and stops BEFORE index 4. So the output is `['Green', 'Blue', 'Yellow']`. Negative indexing is cool too: `colors[-1]` gives the last item, 'Pink'!

exam_tips: 📌 `append()` adds one entire object to the end of a list. `extend()` unpacks a sequence and adds multiple elements one by one.
📌 Dictionary keys CANNOT be lists, because keys must be immutable. Trying to use `{[1,2]: 'Numbers'}` will cause a TypeError.
📌 When looping over a dictionary `for x in my_dict:`, the loop variable `x` will hold the dictionary KEYS, not the values.
quick_recap: ⭐ Lists maintain the order of insertion, but historically, Python Dictionaries did not guarantee order (though they do in modern Python 3.7+).
⭐ The `pop()` method in lists takes an index and returns the removed element.
⭐ To check if a key exists in a dictionary, use the `in` operator: `if 'name' in student:`.
